title: One Particle, Two Slits: How Waves Add, Cancel and Paint Stripes
audience: A curious adult with no background in this field

source.title: Wave interference; 4.7.3: Wave Interference- Standing Waves and Beats; Double-slit experiment; 25.1: The Double-slit Experiment
source.authors: Wikipedia contributors (s1, s3); LibreTexts authors (s2, s4)
source.venue: Wikipedia and LibreTexts (encyclopedia and textbook pages)

intro.summary: These four sources ask what happens when waves overlap, and why that leads to the most puzzling experiment in quantum physics. They show that overlapping waves simply add, so crests meeting crests reinforce and crests meeting troughs cancel. Light sent through two slits makes bright and dark stripes, which is evidence that light behaves like a wave. Even when electrons or photons arrive one at a time, as single dots, the same stripes build up. If you detect which slit each particle used, the stripes disappear. The sources are encyclopedia and textbook summaries, not original research. How to interpret these results is still disputed: Copenhagen, many-worlds, de Broglie–Bohm and relational views all predict the same observations but describe them very differently. This lesson leaves out standing waves, beats, thin films, coherence and interferometry. Good follow-up topics are the quantum eraser, weak measurement, Feynman's path integral and the Mach–Zehnder interferometer.
background: A wave is a repeating disturbance, like a ripple, with crests (high points) and troughs (low points).
The wavelength is the distance from one crest to the next, and the amplitude is how tall the crests are.
For light, what our eyes and detectors register is brightness (intensity), which goes with the square of the amplitude.
In quantum physics, a particle such as an electron is described by a wave whose squared size gives the chance of finding the particle at each place.
intro.aha: Particles fired one at a time each land as a single dot, yet together they build a striped pattern that only waves passing through both slits can make, and finding out which slit each one used wipes the stripes away.

primer.heading: The question
primer.body: Is light a stream of tiny particles or a wave? The question was argued over for centuries. Around 1801 Thomas Young suggested a test: let light pass through two narrow slits and see what lands on a screen behind them. Later, physicists asked the same question about electrons, atoms and even large molecules.
primer.quote: In modern physics, the double-slit experiment demonstrates that light and matter can exhibit behavior associated with both classical particles and classical waves.

primer.heading: The rule behind it: waves add
primer.body: When two waves meet at a point, their disturbances simply add up. If crest meets crest, the result is twice as tall. If crest meets trough, they cancel. The energy is not destroyed: it moves away from the dark spots and into the bright ones.
primer.quote: If the two beams are of equal intensity, the maxima are four times as bright as the individual beams, and the minima have zero intensity.

primer.heading: What was done
primer.body: Light from a laser passes through two slits. At each spot on the screen, light from one slit has travelled a little farther than light from the other, so the two waves arrive more or less in step. Later versions sent electrons, atoms and molecules, sometimes so faintly that only one particle was in the apparatus at a time. Other versions placed detectors at the slits to find out which slit each particle used.

primer.heading: What was found
primer.body: Two slits give alternating bright and dark stripes, which only waves can explain. Each particle still lands as a single dot at one random spot. Yet thousands of dots together trace out the stripes. When detectors reveal which slit each particle went through, the stripes vanish.
primer.quote: The resulting pattern on the screen is the same as if each individual particle had passed through both slits.

primer.heading: Why it matters, and what is unsettled
primer.body: This experiment shows wave–particle duality: matter is detected as particles but spreads and interferes like a wave. The same physics underlies electron microscopes and precise length measurement. The predictions are not in doubt. What the experiment says about reality is still argued over, and the main interpretations disagree on whether a particle 'really' goes through one slit.
primer.quote: The interpretation of quantum mechanics is still an unsolved problem in modern physics (luckily, it does not prevent us from using quantum mechanics in chemistry).

concepts.title: When waves meet, they add
concepts.idea: Two overlapping waves add point by point, so their phase difference decides whether they reinforce (crest on crest) or cancel (crest on trough).

predict.question: Two identical loudspeakers play the same steady note. At your seat, the sound from one speaker arrives exactly one and a half cycles behind the sound from the other. In the ideal case, with no echoes, what do you hear of that note?
options: Twice as loud as one speaker
Very quiet: the two waves cancel
Exactly as loud as one speaker
No way to tell, because the shift is more than one full cycle
why: Two speakers sound as if they should be louder than one. But extra sound only adds up when crests meet crests, and a one-and-a-half-cycle delay puts each crest on a trough.

Right. A delay of one full cycle changes nothing, so one and a half cycles acts like half a cycle. Every crest lands on a trough, and equal waves cancel. In a real room, echoes keep it from being perfectly silent.
The sum equals one wave only at in-between shifts, such as a third of a cycle. One and a half cycles is the full crest-on-trough case, not an in-between one.
The slider stops at one cycle, but waves repeat every cycle. Take away the whole cycles and half a cycle is left, which is the crest-on-trough case.

terms.means: The rule that overlapping waves combine by adding their heights at each point
How far one wave is shifted relative to the other, measured as a fraction of a full cycle (360° or 2π)
Waves lined up crest on crest, adding to a taller wave
Waves lined up crest on trough, cancelling each other

model.title: Two waves on the same stretch of water, and the wave you would actually see
model.note: Teaching model: a frozen snapshot of two waves with the same wavelength and the same height, drawn along a line. The slider shifts wave 2 by an angle in degrees (360° is one full cycle, 2π in the paper's notation). Real waves move, can differ in height and spread in two or three dimensions. Numbers are illustrative, not measured data.

x.label: Position along the water (in wave lengths)

series.label: Wave 2
series.expr: amp * cos(2 * pi * x + phi * pi / 180)

series.label: Both together
series.expr: amp * cos(2 * pi * x) + amp * cos(2 * pi * x + phi * pi / 180)

steps.say: Picture two ripples crossing the same stretch of water. This dashed curve is wave 1.
This dashed curve is wave 2. It is the same size and the same length as wave 1.
The solid curve is what you would actually see: the water with both waves present at once.
This slider slides wave 2 along the water. Watch the solid curve change shape.
This slider makes both waves taller or shorter together.
This box tells you how tall the combined wave gets.

explore.prompt: You have seen the two extremes. Now look for the shifts in between, and use both sliders.

goals.text: Make the combined wave exactly as tall as one wave on its own.
hints: Lined up gives double height. Crest on trough gives nothing. You want something in between.
Slide wave 2 slowly between lined up and crest on trough, and watch the 'Combined ÷ one wave' box.
The spot is past a quarter of a cycle but before half a cycle.

goals.text: Make each single wave taller than 1, yet keep the combined wave only 1.5 high.
hints: Tall waves that line up add to more than 1.5. Something has to take height away.
Shift wave 2 so its crests partly meet wave 1's troughs, then adjust the height.
With both waves at their tallest, you need the sum to be as tall as one wave. That is the same shift as in the first goal.

feedback.correct: Yes. Waves repeat every cycle, so a delay of one and a half cycles works like a delay of half a cycle. Crest meets trough, and two equal waves cancel. Real rooms add echoes, so the quiet spot is not perfectly silent.
feedback.incorrect: What matters is where the crests land, not the total delay. Take away the whole cycles from one and a half and half a cycle is left. That puts every crest on a trough, so equal waves cancel. Echoes in a real room keep the silence from being perfect.

steps.say: Start with the crests lined up. Each crest of wave 1 sits exactly on a crest of wave 2.
At every point, the water's height is wave 1's height plus wave 2's height. This point-by-point adding is called superposition.
Crest plus crest gives a crest twice as tall: the combined wave reaches the 'twice one wave' line. This reinforcing is called constructive interference.
Now slide wave 2 a quarter of a cycle. How far one wave is shifted against the other is the phase difference. The crests now miss each other, and the sum is only about 1.41 tall.
Slide it to half a cycle. Every crest of wave 2 now lands on a trough of wave 1. Up plus down gives zero everywhere, so the water is flat. This is destructive interference.
Keep going to a full cycle. Crest is back on crest, and the height is double again. Shifting by a whole cycle is the same as not shifting at all.
Back to half a cycle, with both waves made taller. The water is still flat. Equal waves that meet crest on trough cancel, whatever their size.

understand.explanation: When two waves overlap, the water or air simply adds their heights at each point. So the result depends on how the waves are lined up. Crest on crest gives a wave as tall as the two added together. Crest on trough gives the difference between their heights, which is zero for equal waves. Shifts in between give in-between heights. A shift of a whole cycle (2π) changes nothing, so any whole number of cycles reinforces and any odd number of half-cycles cancels. The sources work this out by adding two cosine waves with a trigonometric rule. They also point to everyday cases, such as loud and quiet spots near a stereo and the throbbing hum of twin jet engines. Cancelling at one spot does not destroy energy: the sources note that it moves to other places.
understand.quote: If a crest of a wave meets a crest of another wave of the same frequency at the same point, then the amplitude is the sum of the individual amplitudes—this is constructive interference. If a crest of one wave meets a trough of another wave, then the amplitude is equal to the difference in the individual amplitudes—this is known as destructive interference.

connect.caption: This is the paper's formula for the sum of two equal waves (Wave interference, Real-valued wave functions). A is the height of each wave, set by the height slider. φ is the shift of wave 2, set by the shift slider; 360° on the slider equals 2π here. The factor 2A·|cos(φ/2)| is the height of the combined wave shown in the box. It is 2A when φ is 0 or 2π, and 0 when φ is π. The second cosine is the shape of the wave itself. The model freezes time t to draw a snapshot.

activities.prompt: The same two waves at two different shifts. Compare the solid combined wave in each.
activities.takeaway: Nothing about the waves themselves changed, only how they are lined up. That alone swings the result from double height to completely flat.

concepts.recap: Overlapping waves add point by point. Lined up crest on crest they double, crest on trough they cancel, and in-between shifts give in-between heights.

concepts.title: Brightness: four times as bright, or completely dark
concepts.idea: Detectors see intensity, the square of the summed wave, so two equal beams give I₁ + I₂ + 2√(I₁I₂)cos(φ): up to four times one beam's brightness where they agree and zero where they cancel, with energy moved rather than lost.

predict.question: Three equal beams of light all arrive perfectly in step at one spot. Each beam alone would make that spot 1 unit bright. How bright is the spot now?
options: 3 units
6 units
9 units
It goes dark
why: Tempting if you add brightnesses directly. But brightness only adds that way for beams that ignore each other. Here the wave heights add first, to three times one beam's height.
Tempting if you double the plain sum, the way two beams gave 4 instead of 2. The rule is not 'double it': brightness is the square of the total height, and that height is three times one beam's.
Right. In step, the three heights add to 3A, and brightness is the square: (3A)² = 9A², nine times one beam. The extra light comes from darker spots elsewhere in the pattern.
Tempting if you remember that waves can cancel. But cancelling needs crests meeting troughs. Here every crest meets a crest, so the waves reinforce.

terms.means: How bright light is where it lands: the square of the wave's height, averaged over time
The extra part, 2√(I₁I₂)cos φ, that makes the total brighter or dimmer than the plain sum; averaged over a full cycle it is zero

model.title: Brightness where two beams meet
model.note: Teaching model: two ideal beams of one colour with the same polarization and a fixed phase difference. Brightness is in arbitrary units, where 1 means one beam glowing alone. Phase difference is measured in multiples of π. The curve follows the sources' formula exactly; slider values are illustrative, not measured data.

outputs.label: Brightness at the marker
outputs.expr: max(0, b1 + b2 + 2 * sqrt(b1 * b2) * cos(pi * phi))

series.label: Both beams together
series.expr: max(0, b1 + b2 + 2 * sqrt(b1 * b2) * cos(pi * x))

steps.say: This curve shows how bright the screen is where two beams of light meet. Each point along the bottom is a different phase difference.
These two sliders set how bright each beam would be on its own. The thin lines mark those single-beam levels.
The dashed line is the plain sum: what you'd see if the two beams simply ignored each other.
This slider moves the marker to one phase difference, and this box reads the brightness there.

explore.prompt: Now steer the stripes yourself. Use the beam sliders to shape how bright and how dark the pattern gets.

goals.text: Make the brightest spot exactly 2 units while the darkest spot still goes completely dark
hints: For a spot to go completely dark, what has to be true about the two beams?
Equal beams make the brightest spot four times one beam alone. Work backwards from the 2 you want.
Both beams must match, and each must be well below 1. The brightest spot equals 4 × one beam.

goals.text: Keep both beams switched on, but make even the darkest stripes glow at least a quarter as bright as the brighter beam alone
hints: Dark spots need the two waves to cancel. When can't they cancel completely?
Leave beam 1 where it is and make beam 2 much dimmer. Watch the darkest-spot box.
Try beam 2 at a quarter of beam 1's brightness or less, but not zero.

feedback.correct: Yes. In step, the three wave heights add to three times one height. Brightness is the square of the height, so the spot is 3² = 9 times as bright. The light comes from darker spots nearby, so the total is conserved.
feedback.incorrect: The trap is adding brightnesses directly. Waves add their heights first, and only then does the detector square the total. Three equal heights in step make 3A, and (3A)² is nine times one beam. That extra light is borrowed from darker places in the pattern.

steps.say: Start with two equal beams, each 1 unit bright on its own, meeting crest on crest. You might expect the screen to read 2. It reads 4.

Why 4? Detectors can't follow light's fast wiggle. They record the square of the wave's height, averaged over time: this is called intensity. Crest on crest doubles the height, and squaring that gives four times the brightness.
Now slide a quarter cycle out of step. The screen reads 2, exactly the plain sum, as if the beams were ignoring each other.
Half a cycle out of step, crest meets trough. The heights cancel and the screen goes completely dark.

Is light destroyed? No. The curve rises above the dashed plain sum as far as it dips below it, so the average stays 2. That swing is the interference term, 2√(I₁I₂)cos φ: it moves light from dark spots to bright ones.
Now dim beam 2 and watch the dark spot. A weaker wave can't fully cancel a stronger one, so even the darkest place still glows.
With unequal beams, the brightest stripes fall short of four times and the darkest never reach zero. The stripes turn paler, while the average stays at the plain sum.

understand.explanation: Light wiggles far too fast for any detector to follow, so what we actually see is intensity: the square of the wave's height, averaged over time. Because of that squaring, two equal beams meeting in step are not twice as bright as one beam but four times, and half a cycle out of step they give zero. The sources write the rule as I = I₁ + I₂ + 2√(I₁I₂)cos(φ). They note that energy is not lost at dark spots but redistributed to other areas, so averaged across the pattern the brightness equals the plain sum. When the beams are unequal, the extra term can never cancel the whole plain sum, so dark stripes stay faintly lit. All of this assumes ideal, steady waves with the same polarization; the sources stress that mismatched polarizations, or ordinary light sources that mix many frequencies, wash the stripes out.
understand.quote: Thus, the interference pattern maps out the difference in phase between the two waves, with maxima occurring when the phase difference is a multiple of 2π. If the two beams are of equal intensity, the maxima are four times as bright as the individual beams, and the minima have zero intensity.

connect.caption: I is the brightness at the marker. I₁ and I₂ are each beam's brightness alone, set by the two beam sliders. φ is the phase difference, which the source writes as φ₁(r) − φ₂(r); the model measures it in multiples of π. The first two terms make the dashed plain sum. The last term is the interference term, which swings between +2√(I₁I₂) and −2√(I₁I₂).

concepts.recap: Detectors see the square of the combined wave, so equal beams in step are four times as bright as one and out of step are dark; the light is moved around, not lost.

activities.title: From double the height to four times the brightness

steps.text: One beam alone has wave height A. Its brightness is the square of that height. Call it 1 unit.
A second, equal beam arrives exactly in step, crest on crest. The heights add.
The detector squares the total height, not each beam separately.
Shift one beam half a cycle, so crest meets trough. The heights cancel.
Averaged over every phase difference, the cos φ part is zero. Only the two beams' own brightness remains.

activities.takeaway: Squaring turns 'twice the height' into 'four times the brightness'. The extra light in the bright spots is exactly the light missing from the dark ones.

concepts.title: Two slits paint stripes
concepts.idea: At each spot on the screen the waves from the two slits have travelled different distances, so their phase difference changes across the screen and makes evenly spaced bright and dark fringes, spaced about w = zλ/d.

predict.question: In the source's worked example, slits 0.5 mm apart lit by 0.6 μm light make bright stripes 1.2 mm apart on a screen 1 m away. Someone moves the slits closer, to 0.25 mm apart, and keeps the same light and screen. How far apart are the bright stripes now?
options: 0.6 mm
1.2 mm, unchanged
2.4 mm
The stripes disappear
why: It feels natural that closer slits mean closer stripes. In fact closer slits make the extra distance grow more slowly across the screen, so the stripes spread out rather than crowding in.
The light and the screen did not change, but the slit gap is the d in w = zλ/d. Changing it changes the spacing.
Right: halving d doubles w. The extra distance now builds up half as fast, so you must go twice as far along the screen to gain one more wave: 2 × 1.2 mm = 2.4 mm.
The two waves still overlap and still have a steadily changing extra distance, so stripes still form. They are just wider apart.

terms.means: How much farther the wave from one slit travels than the wave from the other to reach the same spot
The alternating bright and dark stripes that interference paints on the screen
The distance between neighbouring bright stripes, about w = zλ/d

model.title: Brightness across the screen behind two slits
model.note: Teaching model: the far-field, small-angle version with very narrow slits, so the slower brightness envelope from each slit's width is left out. It uses two equal beams of a single wavelength, and brightness is shown in units of one slit alone. The default settings are the source's worked example (0.5 mm, 0.6 μm, 1 m giving 1.2 mm). Other settings are illustrative.

outputs.label: Extra distance at the marked spot

steps.say: Light passes through two narrow slits and lands on a screen. This curve shows how bright each spot on the screen is.
The flat line is how bright the screen would be with only one slit open.
This slider sets the wavelength of the light. Watch the stripes change.
This one sets how far apart the two slits are.
This one moves the screen nearer or farther. The box reports the gap between bright stripes.

explore.prompt: You are the experimenter now. Tune the light and the slits to paint the stripes you want.

goals.text: Without moving the screen, spread the bright stripes so they sit about 2 mm apart (between 1.9 and 2.1 mm).
hints: Leave the screen distance alone. Which other two sliders change the gap between stripes?
Longer waves spread the stripes, and so do slits that sit closer together. You need about 1.7 times the current gap.
Even the reddest light here cannot spread the stripes enough on its own. Keep the colour and bring the slits closer than they are now.

goals.text: The marked spot starts out dark. Make it a bright stripe by changing only the distance between the slits.
hints: The spot is dark because the extra distance there is a half-number of waves, so crest meets trough.
Change the slit gap and watch the extra-distance box. A bright spot needs a whole number of waves.
Narrowing the gap a little shrinks the extra distance. Aim for the whole number just below where it starts.

feedback.correct: Yes. The spacing is w = zλ/d, so halving the slit gap doubles it, from 1.2 mm to 2.4 mm. With the slits closer, the extra distance grows more slowly across the screen.
feedback.incorrect: It is tempting to think closer slits give closer stripes. But the stripe spacing depends on how fast the extra distance builds up along the screen. Closer slits build it up more slowly, so w = zλ/d gets bigger: 2.4 mm.

steps.say: Start with the source's own example: slits 0.5 mm apart, 0.6 μm light, screen 1 m away. At the centre, both slits are equally far away, so their waves arrive in step. The result is bright, four times one slit alone.
Now look 3 mm out. The far slit's wave has travelled 2.5 wavelengths farther, so crest meets trough and the spot is dark. That extra travel is the path difference.
Moving along the screen, the path difference grows steadily. It passes a whole number of waves (bright), then a half number (dark), again and again. These stripes are fringes.
The distance from one bright fringe to the next is the fringe spacing. Here it is 1.2 mm, the same number the source works out.
Make the waves longer. You now have to go farther out before the path difference reaches one whole wave, so the fringes spread apart.
Back to 0.6 μm, but now push the slits wider apart. The path difference grows faster across the screen, so the fringes crowd together.
Return the slits to 0.5 mm and move the screen twice as far away. The same angles now cover more screen, so the spacing doubles to 2.4 mm.
Put it all together: red light, slits close together, a far screen. The fringes become broad bands several millimetres wide. All three effects follow one rule: w = zλ/d.

understand.explanation: Behind two narrow slits, every spot on the screen receives one wave from each slit. Away from the centre, one slit is a little farther away. That path difference sets the phase difference between the two waves. Where the path difference is a whole number of wavelengths, the waves add and the spot is bright. Where it is a half number, they cancel and the spot is dark. Because the path difference grows steadily along the screen, the fringes repeat evenly, about w = zλ/d apart: longer waves or a farther screen spread them, and wider-spaced slits crowd them. This is the source's far-field, small-angle formula. It gives 1.2 mm for 0.5 mm slits, 0.6 μm light and a 1 m screen. Real slits also have a width, which adds a slower brightness envelope that this model leaves out. Thomas Young described this kind of experiment in 1801 as part of his case for light being a wave.
understand.quote: When the two waves are in phase, i.e. the path difference is equal to an integral number of wavelengths, the summed amplitude, and therefore the summed intensity is maximum, and when they are in anti-phase, i.e. the path difference is equal to half a wavelength, one and a half wavelengths, etc., then the two waves cancel and the summed intensity is zero.

connect.caption: The source's fringe-spacing formula, w = zλ/d. Here w is the gap between bright stripes (the output box), z is the slit-to-screen distance, λ is the wavelength and d is the distance between the slits. With z in metres, λ in micrometres and d in millimetres, w comes out in millimetres. The formula holds when the screen is far away compared with the slit gap.

concepts.recap: The extra distance from the two slits grows steadily across the screen, painting evenly spaced bright and dark stripes about w = zλ/d apart.

concepts.title: One particle at a time, the stripes still appear
concepts.idea: Each particle lands at a single random spot whose chance follows the two-slit brightness pattern, so the stripes are invisible after a few hits and emerge only as many dots pile up.

predict.question: A lab can only afford short runs: it sends 10 particles through the two slits, records where they land, and repeats this 100 times on different days. Then it stacks all 100 screens on top of each other. What does the stacked picture show?
options: Still a blur, because each run of 10 was too small to show stripes
Clear stripes, just like a single run of 1,000 particles
Stripes, but blurrier than a single run of 1,000, because the runs were separate
A single smooth hump, as if each particle used only one slit
why: Tempting, because each run on its own really is a blur. But the dots do not belong to a run: stacked together they are 1,000 independent landings, and 1,000 is enough to show the stripes.
Right. Each particle lands on its own, with the same two-slit odds every time. So 100 runs of 10 give the same statistics as one run of 1,000, and the stripes stand out.

It seems natural that separate runs should add extra blur. But nothing links one particle to the next: each landing follows the same odds whether it came on Monday or Friday, so the stacked pile is as sharp as one long run.
Sending particles one at a time does not close a slit. With both slits open, each particle's landing chance still follows the striped two-slit pattern, not a single-slit hump.

terms.means: How likely an outcome is; here, how likely a particle is to land in each part of the screen
A pattern that exists only in the counts of many random events, not in any single one
The finding that light and matter show both wave and particle properties: they arrive as single dots, but where they land follows a wave pattern

model.title: Where single particles land behind two slits
model.note: Teaching model: the two-slit curve from the previous concept (very narrow slits, far field, one wavelength), with every particle landing independently of the others. The screen is cut into 0.2 mm patches, and a brightest patch collects about 1/30 of all hits. This is approximate: it assumes roughly whole stripes fit on the 12 mm screen. Counts are rescaled so the average pile has the same height as the brightness curve. The dashed band is the average count plus or minus two typical random deviations. That is a bell-curve approximation to counting noise, and it is rough when there are only a few hits. Particle counts and bands are illustrative, not data from any experiment.

outputs.label: Average hits in a brightest 0.2 mm patch
Chance a brightest patch gets no hits at all
Lowest likely reading at a bright stripe
Typical scatter at a bright stripe (share of its height)

y.label: Pile of hits (× one slit alone)

series.label: Where hits pile up on average
Upper edge of usual scatter
series.expr: 4 * cos(pi * d * x / (z * lambda))^2 + 2 * sqrt(480 * cos(pi * d * x / (z * lambda))^2 / n_particles)

series.label: Lower edge of usual scatter
series.expr: max(0, 4 * cos(pi * d * x / (z * lambda))^2 - 2 * sqrt(480 * cos(pi * d * x / (z * lambda))^2 / n_particles))

steps.say: Same screen, same two slits, same three sliders. The solid curve is the stripe pattern you already know. Now we read it as where particles pile up on average.
New slider: how many particles we send, one at a time. Each one lands as a single dot somewhere on the screen.
The dashed lines mark how far a real run's pile usually strays from the average. Watch how wide that band is right now.

explore.prompt: Play with the number of particles. Find where the bright stripes stop being drowned by randomness and start to stand out on their own.

goals.text: Find the smallest particle count, to within about 100, at which even the lowest likely reading at a bright stripe clears the average line.
hints: More particles shrink the dashed band. You want the point where it first clears the line, not the far end of the slider.
Watch the 'Lowest likely reading at a bright stripe' box and the 'Average over the screen' line. Move in big steps first, then small ones.
It happens past a few hundred particles but well before a thousand.

feedback.correct: Yes. Every particle lands independently, with the same two-slit odds. Stacking 100 runs of 10 gives 1,000 landings with exactly the statistics of one run of 1,000, so the stripes show just as clearly.
feedback.incorrect: You probably pictured the stripes as something each run builds for itself. In fact the stripes live only in the odds for each landing. Nothing links one particle to the next, so it doesn't matter whether 1,000 dots come in one run or in a hundred: the pile looks the same.

steps.say: Ten particles. A brightest patch expects only a third of a hit, so about 72% of the time it gets nothing at all, exactly like a dark patch.
The dashed band runs from zero to off the top of the chart. A run this small could look like almost anything. Ten dots cannot tell you where the bright stripes are.
A hundred particles. A bright patch now expects about three hits, but the band still touches zero at the bright stripes. Some bright patches will still come up nearly empty.
Five hundred. Now even an unlucky bright stripe should pile up above the screen's average. The stripes become readable from the dots alone.
Two thousand: four times as many particles, and the scatter has only halved. Random noise shrinks with the square root of the count.
Five thousand. The band hugs the curve. No single dot was predictable, but each one's probability of landing follows the brightness curve. The stripes are a statistical pattern.

Now bring the slits closer. The pile spreads into wider stripes. Each lone particle's odds depend on how far apart both slits are: this is wave–particle duality, dots that pile up into a wave pattern.

understand.explanation: When particles are sent one at a time, each lands as a single dot at one spot, and you cannot predict which. What you can predict is the chance of each spot, and that chance follows the two-slit brightness curve. With a few dots, randomness swamps the stripes. Only as many dots pile up do the bright and dark bands emerge, and the noise shrinks slowly, with the square root of the count. This has been seen directly: G. I. Taylor dimmed light until photons arrived mostly one at a time (1909). Merli, Missiroli and Pozzi (1974) and later Frabboni's group (2012) watched single electrons build the pattern dot by dot. The same holds for atoms and molecules of up to 2,000 atoms. These experiments show what happens, but not why each dot lands where it does. That question is still debated.
understand.quote: This demonstrates the wave–particle duality, which states that all matter exhibits both wave and particle properties: The particle is measured as a single pulse at a single position, while the modulus squared of the wave describes the probability of detecting the particle at a specific place on the screen giving a statistical interference pattern.

check.task: At 500 particles, read the typical scatter at a bright stripe. Now find a particle count that cuts that scatter to less than half, using no more than about 2,100 particles.
check.hint: Random scatter shrinks with the square root of the count. Ask how many times more particles you need to halve it.
check.misconception: Doubling the number of particles halves the scatter. In fact halving the scatter takes about four times as many particles.

connect.caption: The middle part is the source's rule: the chance of finding a particle in a stretch of screen is the integral of |Ψ|², the squared wave (s1). For two narrow slits it has the cos² stripe shape set by d, z and λ, the sliders from before. N, the new slider, multiplies that chance to give the average pile per patch. The last part, scatter ≈ √(expected hits), is the model's counting-noise rule, not the sources'.

concepts.recap: Each particle lands at one unpredictable spot. Its odds follow the two-slit stripes, so the stripes appear only in the pile of many dots.

concepts.title: Knowing the path wipes out the stripes
concepts.idea: The stripes come from the interference term between the two slits' waves. Gaining which-slit information shrinks that term, and full information leaves only the plain sum of two single-slit patterns.

predict.question: No detector this time. Each slit gets a polarizing filter, with the two turned at right angles, so the light itself records which slit it left. Nobody ever measures that record. What happens to the stripes?
options: They stay, because nobody reads the polarization
They fade away, leaving the plain sum of the two slits
They keep full contrast but shift sideways
The whole screen dims, but the stripes keep full contrast
why: It feels as if a person must look. But what matters is whether the set-up records which slit was used. The source says the standard account is independent of any conscious observer.
Right. The polarization holds full which-slit information, so the interference term vanishes. The source reports that crossed polarizers before the slits eliminate the pattern.
A sideways shift would come from changing the path difference between the slits. A record of the path does not shift the stripes. It shrinks the term that makes them.
Contrast is exactly what the record removes. The total light stays at the plain sum, while the up-and-down swing around it disappears.

terms.means: The part of the brightness that swings above and below the plain sum of the two slits, set by the waves' phase difference
How well something in the set-up records which slit a particle went through, from none to complete
Stripe contrast: (brightest − darkest) ÷ (brightest + darkest). It is 1 for perfect stripes and 0 for none

model.title: Brightness across the screen behind two slits, with a detector at the slits
model.note: Teaching model: the far-field, small-angle version with very narrow slits, so each slit alone gives a flat brightness of 1 and the 'plain sum of two single-slit patterns' is a flat line at 2. In real experiments each slit's own pattern is a broad diffraction hump. Stripe contrast falls as √(1 − info²), the textbook best case of the visibility–distinguishability trade-off inequality the source mentions. The source names that inequality but does not give its formula, and real detectors can wash the stripes out faster. Default distances are the source's worked example (0.5 mm, 0.6 μm, 1 m); everything else is illustrative, not measured data.

controls.label: How much the detector reveals about the slit used

series.label: Both slits open
series.expr: 2 + 2 * sqrt(max(0, 1 - info^2)) * cos(2 * pi * d * x / (z * lambda))

series.label: Plain sum of two slits (no stripes)

steps.say: This is the same screen as before: brightness across the screen behind two open slits, with stripes peaking at four times one slit's light.
New: a detector sits at the slits. This slider sets how much it reveals about which slit each particle went through, from nothing to everything.
The dashed line is what you would get by simply adding the light from each slit. Watch the stripes as the detector reveals more.

explore.prompt: Play with the detector. Find out how much path knowledge it takes to dim the stripes, and how little it costs at first.

goals.text: Make the brightest stripes about three times as bright as one slit alone
hints: The brightest stripe is the plain sum plus the stripes' swing above it. How big must that swing be?
The swing is twice the stripe contrast, so you need the contrast to fall to about one half. Watch the contrast box.
Contrast falls slowly at first, so the detector has to reveal well over half before it gets there.

goals.text: Let the detector reveal as much as you can while the stripe contrast stays above 90%
hints: Start from no detector and slide up slowly, watching the contrast box.
Contrast barely drops at first. A detector that reveals a fair amount still leaves strong stripes.
The contrast crosses 90% somewhere between a third and a half on the detector slider.

feedback.correct: Yes. What wipes out the stripes is that the set-up records which slit was used, not that a person looks. Crossed polarizers carry full which-path information, so the interference term vanishes and only the plain sum of the two slits remains.
feedback.incorrect: The stripes do not depend on someone reading the record, and a record does not shift or dim them uniformly. Which-path information shrinks the interference term itself. Full information, like crossed polarizers, removes it and leaves only the plain sum.

steps.say: Start with no detector. The stripes swing all the way from 4 down to 0 times one slit's light.
The dashed line at 2 is the plain sum of the two slits. Everything above and below it is the interference term, the 2√(I₁I₂)cos φ part you met earlier.
Now let the detector reveal a little about which slit each particle used. That record is called which-path information. The stripes get only slightly shallower.
The contrast box measures how deep the stripes are: (brightest − darkest) ÷ (brightest + darkest). This is the visibility. At half the information it is still about 0.87.
Reveal much more. The visibility drops below one half, and even the darkest stripes now get more light than one slit alone.
Full which-path information: the interference term is gone. The curve sits flat on the dashed line, the plain sum of two single slits.
Notice what did not happen. The light did not vanish, and the stripes did not shift. The average stays at 2. Knowing the path removed only the swing that made the stripes.

understand.explanation: The stripes are the interference term riding on top of the plain sum of the two slits' light. A detector that records which slit a particle used shrinks that term. Partial knowledge gives fainter stripes, and complete knowledge removes them, leaving just the sum of two single-slit patterns. Experiments with detectors at the slits find exactly this. A 1987 experiment showed that partial path information can be gained without destroying the interference altogether, a trade-off written as an inequality between fringe visibility and how distinguishable the paths are. The exact shape of the trade-off in this model is the textbook best case, not a measured curve. The source also stresses that the standard account does not need a conscious observer: what matters is whether the set-up physically records the path.
understand.quote: However, such experiments demonstrate that particles do not form the double-slit interference pattern if one detects which slit they pass through; the pattern instead becomes the sum of two single-slit interference patterns.

check.task: Set up a screen where the bright stripes sit 2.4 mm apart and are still visible, but the darkest spots get about as much light as one slit alone.
check.hint: Two different things are asked for. One slider sets how far apart the stripes are; a different one sets how faded they are.
check.misconception: That path information spreads out or shifts the stripes. It leaves their spacing alone and only shrinks their contrast, while spacing still depends on wavelength and distances.

connect.caption: This is the source's two-beam brightness equation with one addition from the model: the factor V (stripe contrast, or visibility) on the interference term. With no detector V = 1, which gives the source's original equation. As the detector reveals more, V shrinks. At full information V = 0, and only I₁ + I₂, the plain sum, is left.

concepts.recap: Which-path information shrinks the interference term: partial knowledge fades the stripes, full knowledge leaves only the plain sum of two slits.

activities.prompt: Three detectors at the same two slits. Compare the stripe contrast and the darkest stripes.

cases.label: Full detector: plain sum, no stripes

activities.takeaway: The trade-off is gradual, not a switch. More path knowledge means a smaller interference term, until full knowledge leaves only the plain sum.

concepts.title: Same results, rival stories
concepts.idea: The main interpretations of quantum mechanics agree on every observed result of the double-slit experiment but disagree about what happens between the source and the screen, so the meaning remains an open question.

terms.means: A story about what is really going on behind the mathematics. Rival interpretations predict the same results.
A family of views from Bohr, Heisenberg, Born and others. Outcomes are truly random, and an experiment shows wave behaviour or particle behaviour, never both at once.
The view that the wavefunction never collapses, so reality branches into parallel versions that interact only through interference.
In de Broglie–Bohm theory, a real wave that passes through both slits and steers a particle that has a definite position.

concepts.recap: Every interpretation agrees on the dots, the stripes and the vanishing stripes. They disagree about what the particle does in between, and that question is still open.

understand.explanation: Every serious account of the double-slit experiment agrees on what the screen shows. Each particle lands as a single dot. Many dots pile up into stripes that only waves passing through both slits can make. Finding out which slit each particle used wipes the stripes away. An interpretation is a story about what happens in between, and here the stories split. In the Copenhagen interpretation, asking 'which slit?' has no meaning without a detector. In de Broglie–Bohm theory, the particle takes one slit, steered by a pilot wave that goes through both. In the many-worlds interpretation, nothing ever collapses and branches of reality interfere. In the relational interpretation, a result describes the interaction between a device and the particle, not a property the particle has on its own. These stories reproduce the same observed patterns (de Broglie–Bohm only under an extra assumption about how starting positions are spread), so this experiment alone cannot pick a winner. The sources call interpretation an unsolved problem, though it does not stop anyone from using the theory.
understand.quote: The interpretation of quantum mechanics is still an unsolved problem in modern physics (luckily, it does not prevent us from using quantum mechanics in chemistry).
understand.quote_where: 25.1: The Double-slit Experiment, "Which way" experiment section

activities.prompt: One electron leaves the source with both slits open and no detectors, and it lands as a dot on the screen. Here are two stories about its journey.

cases.label: Copenhagen interpretation
cases.text: Quantum mechanics is random at its core. Probabilities come from the square of the wave (the Born rule). An experiment can show particle behaviour (a definite slit) or wave behaviour (stripes), but not both at once. With no detector, 'which slit did it go through?' is a question with no meaning. Caveat: the name covers a collection of views, and there is no single definitive statement of it.

cases.label: de Broglie–Bohm theory (pilot wave)
cases.text: The electron always has a precise position, so it really goes through one slit. A pilot wave goes through both slits and guides it, and that is where the stripes come from. The theory is deterministic, yet it gives the same statistics as standard quantum mechanics if the starting positions are spread according to the wave's squared size. It does not fit easily with special relativity.

activities.takeaway: Same dot, same stripes. One story says the path question has no answer. The other says there is a definite path we simply don't know.

activities.prompt: Two more stories, each telling a different tale about the same unseen journey.

cases.label: Many-worlds interpretation
cases.text: Reality is the wavefunction, and it never collapses. There are many parallel branches that interact only through interference. David Deutsch says that in each branch the particle goes through one slit, and interference with its counterparts in other branches makes the stripes. Another advocate, David Wallace, disagrees: in the ordinary double-slit setup the two paths are not separated enough for talk of parallel universes to make sense. Supporters argue among themselves too.

cases.label: Relational interpretation (Carlo Rovelli)
cases.text: A result is not an absolute property of the electron. It comes from the interaction between the electron and whatever measures it. A detector at a slit gains position information, which constrains where the electron can land. If the only interaction happens at the screen, there is no path information, and the landing spots follow the full two-slit pattern.

activities.takeaway: None of these views needs a conscious mind: the 'observer' is any measuring device. And none of them changes what the screen shows.

activities.prompt: Match each interpretation to its story about the particle between the source and the screen.

pairs.target: Without a detector, 'which slit?' has no meaning; an experiment shows wave or particle behaviour, never both at once.
pairs.feedback: Copenhagen-type views rest on complementarity: a set-up reveals one face or the other. They treat the path question as meaningless when nothing records the path.

pairs.target: The wavefunction never collapses; the stripes come from interference between branches of reality.
pairs.feedback: The common thread in many-worlds is a wavefunction that always evolves smoothly, with no collapse. Parallel branches interact only through interference.

pairs.target: The particle always has a precise position and goes through one slit; a wave through both slits steers it.
pairs.feedback: This is the pilot-wave picture. The particle is real and located at every moment, and the guiding wave carries the two-slit information.

pairs.target: A result describes an interaction between a measuring device and the particle, not a property the particle has on its own.
pairs.feedback: Rovelli's view moves the facts into relations. What a device finds depends on how it interacted with the particle.

hints: Look for the one view where the particle has a definite path all along.
The view that rejects collapse entirely is the one with branches.
activities.takeaway: Four stories about the same trip. They differ only where no detector is looking.

activities.title: Observation or interpretation?
activities.prompt: Sort each statement. Is it something every view accepts because experiments show it, or is it one view's story about what happens unseen?

cards.text: Each particle is detected as a single dot at one place on the screen.
cards.feedback: Observed. Light and electrons are always absorbed at discrete points, and every interpretation must reproduce this.

cards.text: Dots sent one at a time slowly build up a striped pattern.
cards.feedback: Observed. It has been seen with photons, electrons, atoms and molecules. Every view accepts it and tries to explain it.

cards.text: When detectors record which slit each particle used, the stripes disappear.
cards.feedback: Observed. With which-slit information, the pattern becomes the sum of two single-slit patterns. The views differ only on why.

cards.text: Running the same set-up again, single dots land in different places; only the overall pattern repeats.
cards.feedback: Observed. The disagreement is about the cause: Copenhagen says the randomness is fundamental, while de Broglie–Bohm says it reflects starting positions we do not know.

cards.text: The particle went through exactly one slit, guided by a wave that went through both.
cards.feedback: Interpretation. This is de Broglie–Bohm theory. Copenhagen-type views would call the path question meaningless here.

cards.text: With no detector, asking which slit the particle used has no meaning.
cards.feedback: Interpretation. This is a Copenhagen-type claim. de Broglie–Bohm theory flatly denies it.

cards.text: The stripes come from interference with versions of the particle in parallel universes.
cards.feedback: Interpretation. This is Deutsch's many-worlds reading, and even fellow many-worlds advocate Wallace doubts it fits this set-up.

cards.text: The detector at the slit makes the wave function collapse to one position.
cards.feedback: Interpretation. One source calls this the simplest reading, but many-worlds says nothing ever collapses.

hints: Ask: could a camera record this, or is it about what happens where nothing is recording?
Anything about collapse, parallel universes, hidden paths or 'meaningless questions' is a story, not a reading on a screen.
activities.takeaway: The left pile is the shared ground any theory must reproduce. The right pile is where the debate lives.

activities.question: Which story about the particle's unseen journey seems most reasonable to you? There is no marked answer; each choice has support and costs.

options.text: Copenhagen: without a detector, the path question has no answer.
options.feedback: Support: it stays close to what is measured and builds in complementarity, which matches the vanishing stripes. Limit: it is a loose family of views with no single definitive statement, and it treats measurement as special without fully saying why.

options.text: de Broglie–Bohm: one slit, steered by a pilot wave.
options.feedback: Support: particles have real positions at all times, and the theory reproduces the standard statistics. Limits: it needs the 'quantum equilibrium' assumption about starting positions, and it does not fit easily with special relativity.

Support: it keeps one simple rule, a smoothly evolving wavefunction, with no special collapse step. Limit: it asks you to accept many parallel branches, and its own advocates disagree about how to apply it to the ordinary double slit.

options.text: Relational: results belong to interactions, not to the particle alone.
options.feedback: Support: it explains why a slit detector changes the pattern, because the interaction itself carries path information. Limit: you give up the idea that the particle has properties independent of anything it interacts with.

options.text: I'd rather not pick: the sources say it's unsolved.
options.feedback: That is a defensible stance. The sources call interpretation an unsolved problem that does not stop practical use of the theory. Remember that these views also go beyond what this one experiment can test.

activities.question: A friend says: "The double-slit experiment proves that each particle literally goes through both slits." What is the best reply?

options.text: Right: the stripes prove it went through both slits.
options.feedback: The stripes are real, but de Broglie–Bohm theory gets the same stripes with the particle going through only one slit. The experiment shows a two-slit pattern; it does not settle what the particle 'literally' did.

options.text: The stripes and their disappearance are agreed facts, but whether the particle 'really' passes through both slits depends on the interpretation, and the experiment alone doesn't settle it.
options.feedback: Yes. Every view agrees on what the screen shows. Particles sent one at a time each land as a single dot, yet together they build stripes that only waves passing through both slits can make, and learning which slit each one used wipes the stripes away. What lies behind that pattern is the open question.

options.text: Wrong: detectors show each particle goes through one slit, so the stripes are an illusion.
options.feedback: Adding slit detectors changes the experiment, and then the stripes vanish. Without detectors, the stripes are a real, repeatable pattern of hits that every view must explain.

options.text: Wrong: it shows that a conscious observer creates the result.
options.feedback: None of these views needs a mind. The standard reading is described as independent of any conscious observer, and in the relational view the 'observer' is the measuring device.

hints: Separate what the screen shows from what someone says happened before the screen.
Is there any interpretation that gets the stripes with only one slit used?
